facts.raw_span: A 50-year-old man
no significant past medical history
1-week history of rapidly progressive gait disturbance
no back pain, fevers, night sweats, or weight loss
full strength throughout all extremities
decreased sensation from the T3 dermatome downward
four beats of clonus bilaterally
hyperreflexia in the lower extremities
profound ataxia, rendering him unable to walk more than a few steps
Contrast-enhanced MRI of the thoracic spine demonstrated a diffusely enhancing lesion centered at T1 with near-circumferential epidural extension causing severe cord compression
CT of the thoracic spine showed an expansile bony lesion of the T1 vertebral body with extension into the left pedicle and posterior elements
CT scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed no evidence of a primary malignancy

rationales.F03: Rapidly progressive gait disturbance suggests a compressive or infiltrative lesion.
rationales.F06: Decreased sensation from the T3 dermatome downward indicates a spinal cord lesion.
rationales.F07: Clonus and hyperreflexia are signs of upper motor neuron lesions, consistent with spinal cord compression.
rationales.F08: Hyperreflexia in the lower extremities is consistent with spinal cord compression.
rationales.F09: Profound ataxia is consistent with spinal cord compression or injury.
rationales.F10: Diffusely enhancing lesion with near-circumferential epidural extension causing severe cord compression is highly suggestive of spinal cord compression due to metastatic tumor or other mass lesion.
rationales.F11: Expansile bony lesion of the T1 vertebral body with extension into the left pedicle and posterior elements is highly suggestive of a metastatic tumor or other malignant process.
rationales.F12: Absence of primary malignancy on CT scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis makes metastatic tumor less likely, but does not rule it out entirely.
